title: Good PD Aims Teacher Thinking Well
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. asks what separates good professional development from lesser PD and answers that the decisive factor is what is happening in the minds of the teachers during the session. Borrowing the logic of good teaching, he says good PD aims learners' attention at things worth thinking about, because people remember what they think about. Topic, speaker and activities all matter, but as instruments for aiming that thinking: an overly abstract topic loses attention, a speaker cannot outsource the aiming to someone else's slides, and varied activities keep attention on the target material. Most important is the degree to which teachers see themselves as their own foremost PD provider, which he frames as a mirror of John Almarode's claim about students as their own teachers. He closes with two takeaways for PD leaders and two for recipients.
points: Good PD, like good teaching, works by aiming learner attention at things worth thinking about, since memory mirrors the quality of thought during learning.
Topic, speaker and activity all matter, but each is a tool for aiming thinking rather than a source of quality in itself.
A speaker cannot rely on excellent slides produced by someone else, because the speaker's words and moves do the aiming; reading from slides is ineffective.
Teachers who see themselves as their own PD provider get the most from any session, and leaders should deliberately build that perspective rather than blame teachers for lacking it.
Recipients should point their thinking at things that deepen understanding of their work and students and take ownership of their own growth.
quotes: What's most important is what's happening in the minds of the teachers during the PD. Good PD, just like good teaching, tends to look like effectively aiming the attention of the learner at things worth thinking about.
Because we remember what we think about. And the way in which we remember it mirrors the quality of thought that was happening when we learned it.

If the topic is too abstract, too complicated, too disconnected from where the teachers' hearts and minds are, then they won't think about it during the PD and will instead think about other things like what to make for dinner tonight or the stack of papers they brought with them for grading.
The slides are a tool for aiming thinking but not the primary means by which the thinking is aimed. The speaker who uses the slides does that.

And of course the activities that happen during the PD matter too -- not because there is any magic in any one activity but because mixing up activities is a means through which a PD speaker can keep teacher thinking aimed at the target material.
But mostly -- even more than the topic or the speaker or the activity -- good PD is influenced by the degree to which the learner conceives of *themselves* as their foremost PD provider.

Just as good teachers must believe they can have an influence on the degree to which their students come to view themselves as their own teachers, so too good PD providers must believe that they can influence the degree to which they can help teachers adopt a similar perspective.
